title: MYP Design Revision: A Practical eAssessment Plan
summary: MYP Design revision made practical. Learn what to practise, how to self-assess with criteria A-D, and how to manage your ePortfolio time with confidence.
body_markdown:
MYP Design revision means practising how to make your decisions visible: identify a need, research it, develop a feasible idea, create a solution and evaluate it using evidence. Preparation should follow that entire cycle.


The MYP Design eAssessment uses an ePortfolio, assessed by your teacher against published criteria and subject to external IB moderation. The final solution matters, but so does the thinking behind it. A polished object cannot explain an undocumented decision. Purposeful research, justified choices and meaningful testing make your design story convincing.


### Your MYP Design revision checklist


Before attempting a complete task, check that you can:


- justify a specific user's need
- plan research and analyse existing solutions
- write measurable specifications
- develop and compare feasible ideas
- communicate a design precisely
- document creation and justify changes
- test against specifications and propose improvements


Use the[MYP Design subject resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-design) to identify gaps. RevisionDojo's Study Notes, Questionbank and Flashcards help you move from understanding terminology to applying it.


### Understand what the criteria measure


Each criterion is awarded an achievement level from 0-8. Follow your school's current task documentation for submission requirements and specific guidance.


Criterion Central question Evidence to practise


A: Inquiring and analysing Do I understand the problem? Need justification, research, product analysis and design brief


B: Developing ideas Is my proposal feasible? Specifications, alternative ideas, selection and detailed communication


C: Creating the solution Can I realise my proposal? Logical planning, technical skill, process evidence and justified changes


D: Evaluating How successful is my solution? Testing, evidence, evaluation, improvements and impact


These stages connect. Research should shape specifications, specifications should guide creation, and testing should establish whether those requirements were met. If a specification disappears after you write it, revisit that connection.


The guides to[MYP criteria across subjects](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-criteria-per-subject) and[criteria A-D explained](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-criteria-a-b-c-d-explained) offer context for interpreting achievement descriptors.


### What to practise for each criterion


### Criterion A: turn inquiry into a focused brief


Practise with a hypothetical problem, such as helping a student organise equipment in a crowded workspace. Identify the user, explain the need and prioritise research into dimensions, materials, safety and behaviour.


When analysing existing products, explain why features succeed or fail for that user. Finish with a brief stating what you intend to design, for whom and why. The[guide to writing a design brief](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-design/myp-design-writing-a-design-brief/notes) helps connect research findings to a clear direction.


Separate information you need from information that is merely interesting. For each research question, record how the answer could influence a design decision. Measuring shelf depth, for example, can establish a size constraint; collecting unrelated product photographs may add little useful evidence.


### Criterion B: make ideas testable


Replace vague specifications with observable requirements. “The organiser should hold five textbooks without permanent deformation” gives you a clearer test than “it should be strong.” Your threshold must come from research.


Generate different concepts and annotate dimensions, materials, mechanisms and user interaction. Compare alternatives against the same specifications before selecting one. Detailed drawings, component lists or interface plans should provide enough information to support creation.


### Criterion C: capture consequential decisions


Build a logical plan covering steps, resources, estimated time and quality checks. During production, capture moments that demonstrate technical skill, progress or an important decision. Explain what changed, why and how it affects your specifications.


A student unveils an elaborate lamp whose cord cannot reach the socket while another student questions whether one feature could provide light


Complexity alone does not demonstrate quality. Choose technical challenges that serve the user and that you can execute safely and competently.


### Criterion D: test your claims


Choose methods that generate useful evidence: capacity measurements, task completion times, observed errors or feedback from relevant users. Asking a friend whether something is “good” gives you little to evaluate.


For each important specification, judge whether it was met fully, partly or not at all, then cite evidence. The[MYP Design evaluating notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-design/myp-design-evaluating/notes) support this distinction between description and evaluation. Recommend improvements that respond directly to findings, explaining how each change would benefit the user.


Record test conditions so your conclusions remain interpretable. If you measure completion time, explain the task, the participant's starting knowledge and any assistance provided. Repeat a measurement where practical, and acknowledge limitations when a small trial cannot establish how every user would respond.


### Self-assess while changes are still possible


Review your work in three passes:


- **Evidence:** Locate where each required strand is addressed.
- **Quality:** Compare that evidence with achievement descriptors, including distinctions between outlining, explaining and justifying.
- **Connections:** Trace requirements from research through specifications, creation and testing.


Create an evidence map recording the page or section for each strand. Add one sentence explaining how it satisfies the descriptor. This exposes the difference between work you remember doing and evidence you actually included.


RevisionDojo's AI Chat and Grading tools can help you question unclear reasoning. Check suggestions against the current rubric, preserve your authentic process and follow your school's academic integrity rules.


### Manage your ePortfolio time


Avoid perfecting inquiry while leaving evaluation unfinished. A practical allocation is 20% for research, 25% for ideas, 30% for creation, 15% for testing and 10% for review. These are planning suggestions, not official IB limits; adapt them to your school's schedule.


End each session with a concrete next action, such as comparing fastening methods against a safety requirement. Keep time before internal deadlines for failed tests, missing images and file checks.


Short practice sessions can isolate weaknesses: write a research plan, refine specifications or design a testing method. Then combine those skills in a longer task.


Keep a simple record of recurring weaknesses after each practice session. If your evaluations repeatedly describe results without explaining them, make interpretation your next target. This gives revision a direction and helps you judge progress through improved evidence rather than hours spent working.


### Build a connected revision routine


Review[MYP Design examples](https://www.revisiondojo.com/coursework-exemplars/subject/myp-design) to understand how evidence supports reasoning. Use them to ask better questions about your own work while developing an independent response.


RevisionDojo brings together Questionbank practice, Study Notes, Flashcards, AI Chat, Grading tools, a Coursework Library and Tutors. Predicted Papers and Mock Exams serve timed assessment preparation; Design preparation should centre on portfolio evidence.


A portfolio argues that your solution grew from inquiry, developed through deliberate choices and survived honest evaluation. Build that argument one decision at a time.
